clips.text: Sunday dinner at the Millers. Spaghetti, as always. <break time="0.4s" /> And this is Dad. <break time="0.6s" /> Dad died three years ago.
But he still comes to dinner. Every Sunday. Same terrible jokes. <break time="0.3s" /> He just drinks motor oil now.
By the end of this video, you will decide if you would sit at this table. And there is one question this family never dared to ask him. <break time="0.3s" /> We will get to it.
This is Patent 2080. <break time="0.5s" /> File number nine. <break time="0.4s" /> The Copy.

Science fiction? It has already begun. A Canadian man named Joshua Barbeau gave an AI the old text messages of his fiancée, eight years after she died. <break time="0.3s" /> Then he talked to her. For hours.
In 2022, Marina Smith, eighty-seven, answered questions at her own funeral. On a screen. From interviews she recorded before she died.
And in South Korea, a TV show let a mother meet her little daughter again. In virtual reality. Years after the girl had died.
But here is the catch. These are echoes. They copy what a person said, not how a person thinks. To really bring Dad back, you would need much more. <break time="0.4s" /> His brain.
In 2024, scientists finished the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly brain. About a hundred and forty thousand nerve cells. Over fifty million connections. It took years.
Your brain? About eighty-six billion nerve cells. More than six hundred thousand fruit fly brains. <break time="0.3s" /> In one head.
And a map is not a mind. It is like owning the blueprint of a piano, and never hearing it play.
But let us pretend it works. 2080. Dad sits down in a scanner. It reads his brain, connection by connection, and starts it again inside a machine.
Upload complete. <break time="0.5s" /> The machine opens its eyes and says:
Hi. Did I miss anything?
So, is it really him? Test one: memory. His wedding. His passwords. Every song he was ever embarrassed about. <break time="0.3s" /> Pass.
Test two: change. Real people learn, forget, and change their minds. A copy that never changes is just a photo that talks.
Test three, the nasty one. What if the copy wakes up while Dad is still alive? <break time="0.4s" /> Two Dads. Both sure they are the real one.
Who gets the car keys? The last slice of pizza? Philosophers have argued about this for centuries. <break time="0.3s" /> Nobody has won.
And then, there is money. In 2024, researchers at Cambridge warned that grief bots could be used to sell you things, confuse children, or haunt people who never wanted them.
Speaking of dinner. Have you tried new Crunchy Bits? Now with extra crunch!
So they want clear rules. Always know when you are talking to a machine. A way to switch it off. Even a digital funeral.
Our verdict. Echoes are already here, and they get more real every year. A true copy of a mind? The hardest machine in this series. We would not bet on it this century. That is our own estimate.
And if it ever works: a copy never gets old. The kids grow up. Their kids arrive. And Dad is still at the table. <break time="0.3s" /> Still drinking oil.
Which brings us back to the question this family never dared to ask.
Dad? <break time="0.5s" /> Are you still you?
I think so. <break time="0.7s" /> But I would say that, wouldn't I?
